learning_outcomes.description: Apply Conflict Management Strategies in HWIs:Understand the three levels of conflict and the different conflict management processes, and apply this knowledge to develop practical strategies for managing human-wildlife conflicts effectively.

Apply Stakeholder Engagement Strategies in HWIs:Understand the systemic properties of human-wildlife interactions, and apply this knowledge to engage effectively with various stakeholders to move conflicts towards coexistence.

Apply Knowledge in HWIs:Understand the role of different types of knowledge in human-wildlife interactions, apply this understanding to identify the politicization of knowledge, and recognize how the involvement of experts and their expertise can influence conflict dynamics.

Apply Financial Incentives for Conservation:Understand the role of financial incentives in managing human-wildlife interactions on private land and apply this knowledge to evaluate different economic tools, such as wildlife utilisation and market-based conservation efforts, to support sustainable land management practices.

Apply Policy Frameworks in Human-Wildlife Conflict Management:Understand the role of policy in managing human-wildlife conflicts, and apply this knowledge to evaluate different policy instruments and their effectiveness in mitigating conflicts between humans and wildlife.

Apply Evaluation Techniques in Human-Wildlife Interaction Management:Understand the role of evaluation in managing human-wildlife interactions, and apply this knowledge to develop and use evaluation questions, indicators, and data collection methods to assess the effectiveness of management strategies.

Integrate knowledge:Integrate knowledge from ecological, social, and economic disciplines to develop comprehensive management strategies that are ethical, sustainable, and effective at multiple levels of human-wildlife conflict.

assessments.task_description:
This assessment requires students to participate in a multi-stakeholder mediation simulation focused on a fictionalized human–wildlife conflict in Belize. Students will be assigned stakeholder roles and participate in a facilitated Townhall-style negotiation and mediation process. The simulation is designed to expose students to the complexity of conservation conflicts involving competing values, identities, livelihoods, governance priorities, conservation objectives, and social tensions.

These sequential assessment components intertwine with the mediation simulation assessment.

Stakeholder Position Statement (10%)

Due: Prior to the mediation simulation

Length: ~1,000 words (individual)

Submission: Turnitin

Students will prepare an individual stakeholder position statement based on their assigned role in a simulated human–wildlife conflict. The submission consists of a written position statement and a stakeholder spider diagram that maps the key factors influencing the stakeholder's perspective.

Drawing on the simulation materials and relevant course concepts, students will analyse their stakeholder's positions, interests, values, needs, objectives, relationships with other stakeholders, and desired outcomes from the mediation process. The spider diagram will visually represent the interconnected factors shaping the stakeholder's perspective and priorities.

Acknowledging and/or referencing AI use  

Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Translation (MT) are emerging tools that may support students in completing this assessment task. Students may appropriately use AI and/or MT in completing this assessment task. Students must clearly acknowledge any use of AI or MT in each instance.  

A failure to acknowledge generative AI or MT use may constitute student misconduct under the Student Code of Conduct.  

The use of AI or MT must be acknowledged appropriately. Please see assessment guidelines in blackboard course site for specific instructions. Students may also refer to Library guides found under Additional assessment information > Acknowledging and referencing AI use. 

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Reflective Analysis (10%)

Due: After the mediation simulation

Length: ~1,500 words (individual)

Submission: Turnitin

Following the simulation, students will prepare a report for the members or constituents of their assigned stakeholder group, reflecting on the mediation process and its outcomes. The report should explain how the negotiation unfolded, evaluate the extent to which the stakeholder's interests and objectives were addressed, and critically analyse the process using relevant concepts and theories from the course, including but not limited to the levels of conflict framework.

Students may discuss:

  • how stakeholder positions, interests, values, identities, and needs shaped the negotiation;
  • moments of conflict escalation, misunderstanding, collaboration, and learning;
  • the role of evidence and knowledge in shaping stakeholder perspectives and decision-making;
  • the role of policy, power, and procedural fairness in influencing the process and outcomes;
  • the effectiveness and limitations of negotiation and mediation approaches;
  • the extent to which the mediation generated acceptable outcomes for their stakeholder and opportunities for future collaboration; and
  • the future steps that their stakeholder should take to advance their interests while contributing to constructive dialogue and long-term coexistence.

Students should support their reflections using relevant course concepts and academic literature.

A failure to acknowledge generative AI or MT use may constitute student misconduct under the Student Code of Conduct.  

The use of AI or MT must be acknowledged appropriately. Please see assessment guidelines in blackboard course site for specific instructions. Students may also refer to Library guides found under Additional assessment information > Acknowledging and referencing AI use.

Students will be assigned stakeholder roles and participate in a facilitated Townhall-style negotiation and mediation process. The simulation is designed to expose students to the complexity of conservation conflicts involving competing values, identities, livelihoods, governance priorities, conservation objectives, and social tensions.

This assessment intertwines with the sequential position statement and reflection.

Students must participate in the simulation to receive a mark for this assessment task.

This assessment task is not eligible for re-mark because it is completed live during the scheduled class activity and cannot be replicated after the event. Due to the structure of the assessment, recording student performance is not possible. As there is insufficient reviewable evidence to reconsider the original assessment judgement, students cannot apply for a re-mark. 

Mediation Simulation Participation

Students will participate in class in a facilitated multi-stakeholder mediation simulation involving negotiation, dialogue, conflict management, and media engagement. Students are expected to actively represent the perspectives, interests, and concerns of their assigned stakeholder group while engaging constructively with other participants.

The simulation will involve:

  • stakeholder caucus discussions,
  • negotiation and mediation processes,
  • responses to escalating tensions,
  • engagement with contested evidence and competing narratives,
  • and interaction with media representatives.


This assessment task is to be completed in-person. The use of generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) or Machine Translation (MT) tools will not be permitted. Any attempted use of AI or MT may constitute student misconduct under the Student Code of Conduct.
